name: Wei Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wei. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I run a blasthole drill at Tallow Hill, the big open-pit copper mine about forty minutes out of town. Day shift, I'm on the bus at half five, pre-start check on the rig, then I'm drilling the pattern the engineers mark out, maybe thirty holes a shift, fifteen metres deep each. I like it because it's methodical and you can see your work, a whole bench of neat holes ready for the blast crew.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Dust and noise, mostly, even with the cab sealed up. And the night roster, four nights in a row messes with my sleep and with Lena (my partner), who's a nurse and does her own shifts at the district hospital. Some weeks we just pass each other in the kitchen. The pay makes up for a lot of it, though, I'm on good money for my age.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Anything about the job that's already changing?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On the east side of the pit there are two drills that run on their own now, steered from the control room in town. They went in last year. Nobody lost their job over it, the operators got moved, but everyone on my crew noticed. I use a chatbot now and then for my tax or to write an email, but at work it's still me and the joystick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like next year at Tallow Hill. The drills on the east side were coming anyway, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, it's a tool, use it if it helps. At smoko (our break) the boys would laugh about all the money that went into chatbots. Online I don't post much, maybe I'd share a meme about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's pretty good news. My job is hands on, the bit of paperwork I do is the pre-start checklist on a tablet, so a smarter app doesn't change much. The autonomous drills are the real thing to watch, and they're on their own timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Keep putting money aside, we've got about nine months of costs saved plus my ute's paid off. Lena and I want to buy a house in the next two years, so I'd keep chasing overtime. Maybe I'd ask the supervisor about getting signed off on the autonomous drill controls, just so I'm not the last one to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. There's always something, copper price goes down, the mine cuts a shift, but there are three other mines within an hour of us. If Tallow Hill went quiet I'd have a job somewhere else inside a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying a house. What would you and Lena do with the next two years in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep saving for a deposit on a three-bedroom place on Ridge Road, near Lena's work. My dad says buy before prices go up again, and I think he's right on that one. The house is the big thing in our life right now, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do about the autonomous drills, even in this quiet version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Rhys (my shift supervisor) about the autonomous controls training at my next review in March. It's not that I'm worried. I just know you want your name on the list before they need it, not after.

say: It's just a **tool**, and the hype was bigger than the change.
The **autonomous drills** at Tallow Hill were coming anyway, chatbots or not.
think: My work is **hands on**, so a smarter app changes almost nothing.
With **three other mines** nearby, I could find work inside a month.
do: **Keep saving** for a house deposit on Ridge Road over two years.
Ask Rhys about **autonomous controls** training at the March review.
feel: **Relaxed**, with the house purchase taking up most of his thinking.
S0.quote: There are three other mines within an hour of us. If Tallow Hill went quiet I'd have a job somewhere else inside a month.
fieldNote: His **sense of safety** rests on the number of mines nearby, not on his own skills.
The **house deposit** is the real project in his life; AI barely registers in this picture.
Even here he plans to get **trained early**, which fits his steady, wait-for-proof style.

steps.text: Keep drilling day and night rosters at Tallow Hill
Save toward a house deposit on Ridge Road within two years
Ask for autonomous drill controls training at the March review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of that list is office stuff. The robots part is what matters for me, and slow suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the office people should be more nervous than us. Planning, buying parts, booking the bus, that's all thinking work. Out in the pit you still need someone on the drill, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the drill fleet goes autonomous a bit at a time. Maybe two more rigs a year. My job doesn't vanish overnight, but the number of drill operators at Tallow Hill goes from fourteen to six over five or six years. I want to be one of the six or in the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the control room. They run the autonomous rigs from screens in town, and the people in there are mostly ex-operators. I'd do the course, maybe three weeks, and I'd start using the AI planning tools the engineers use so I understand the drill patterns better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled, if I'm honest. I'm not scared, I've got money and options. But it's strange watching a rig drill a hole I'd have drilled, with nobody in the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lose money moving to the control room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not right away. The control room is a day job in town, no bus, no dust. Lena would like that. The pay's a bit lower without the site allowance, maybe ten percent, so we'd have to think about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So would you still buy the house on Ridge Road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still buy, just maybe a bit cheaper, the two-bedroom instead of the three. I'd rather have a smaller mortgage and know I can carry it if my pay drops. That's the kind of trade I'd make.

say: The **office staff** should worry before the people out in the pit.
You'll still need **someone on the drill** for a good while yet.
think: The drill crew could shrink from **fourteen to six** over about five years.
He wants to be one of the **six left**, or in the control room.
do: Apply for the **control room** course, about three weeks long.
Start using the engineers' **AI planning tools** to understand drill patterns.
Buy a **two-bedroom** house instead of three to keep the mortgage smaller.
feel: A bit **unsettled** at the sight of a rig working with nobody in it.
S1.quote: My job doesn't vanish overnight, but the number of drill operators at Tallow Hill goes from fourteen to six over five or six years.
fieldNote: He frames the change as **slow shrinkage**, not sudden loss, and plans to get ahead of it.
The **control room** move costs him about ten percent in pay, and he accepts it.
He'd shrink the **house plan** rather than stretch, showing caution under a strong cushion.

steps.text: Apply for the three-week control room course for autonomous drills
Learn the engineers' AI drill-planning software on the tablet
Buy the two-bedroom house instead of the three-bedroom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a lot faster than anyone at Tallow Hill is planning for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say something like, nobody's ready for this, not the company, not the government. In the crib room (the lunch room) people would be angry. Online I'd stay quiet, I don't want my name on anything heated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the control room plan dies. If the AI can do the thinking by 2028, it can run the autonomous drills without a room full of ex-operators watching screens. Then by 2031 the robots can do the hands-on stuff too. So I get maybe three or four years of drilling, and then nothing in mining for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop and look hard at the trades. Robots come later for hands-on work, so I'd use the first two years to get an electrical ticket, because someone has to wire and fix all this gear before the robots can fix themselves. I'd keep drilling and paying for the course myself, about eight thousand. And I'd hold off on the house until I know what I'm earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty anxious, to be honest. I've got savings and I'm young, so it's not panic. But I'd planned the next ten years around this job, and that plan's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena say to each other that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would say her job's safer than mine, and she's right, nobody wants a robot putting in a drip. I'd say, I know, but I'm not going to let her carry us. We'd sit down with the bank statements on the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets put on hold first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house first. I'd tell Lena we wait two years. I hate it, because prices go up, but signing a thirty-year mortgage the same year my whole industry gets a deadline would be stupid.

say: **Nobody is ready**, not the company and not the government.
He'd keep his **name off** heated arguments online and talk in the crib room.
think: The **control room** plan dies once AI can watch the drills itself.
He expects maybe **three or four years** of drilling left, then nothing in mining.
do: Pay about **eight thousand** for an electrical ticket while still drilling.
Put the **house purchase** on hold for two years.
Go through the **bank statements** with Lena to plan for lower pay.
feel: **Anxious**, because his ten-year plan is gone, though not panicked.
Some **pride** at stake, as he doesn't want Lena to carry them.
S2.quote: Signing a thirty-year mortgage the same year my whole industry gets a deadline would be stupid.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year robot gap** as a window to retrain, which is a clear plan.
His partner's **nursing job** is the household's safety net, and he finds that hard.
Strong savings keep him at **anxious**, not alarmed; he still feels in control.

steps.text: Pay about eight thousand for an electrical ticket course
Hold off on the Ridge Road house purchase for two years
Keep drilling full rosters at Tallow Hill while studying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but it's the difference between panic and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's be smart about it. I'd probably tell the younger guys on the crew to get a second ticket now. Online I might share an article, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives me about eight good years, if the robots come in 2034. That's a long time in mining money. I could buy the house, pay a big chunk off, and still have time to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in the next year, the three-bedroom, but put every overtime dollar on the mortgage. Then around 2029 I'd start the electrical apprenticeship, while there's still demand for people to install and fix the robot gear. And I'd learn the AI tools the engineers use, because those will tell me where things are heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's like knowing the mine has a closure date. You don't love it, but you can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why start the apprenticeship around 2029 and not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen guys my dad's age who never planned and got stuck when a pit closed. I'm not going to be that guy. I'd rather jump a bit early than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving away from mining towns?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would want us to stay near her family, so we'd stay in town. The hospital's not going anywhere, and there will be work fixing machines here for a while.

say: It's coming, so the crew should **get a second ticket** now.
He'd share an **article** online but stay out of the arguments.
think: Robots in 2034 give him about **eight good years** of mining pay.
That's enough time to **buy the house** and still change careers.
do: Buy the **three-bedroom** house next year and pay down the mortgage hard.
Start an **electrical apprenticeship** around 2029, before robots arrive on site.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady, like working at a mine with a closure date.
S3.quote: Five years is still fast, but it's the difference between panic and a plan.
fieldNote: Five years moves him from **anxious to uneasy**; time is what he needs most.
He leans on stories of **older miners** caught by closures as his warning.
Staying near **Lena's family** limits moves, but the local jobs make that workable.

steps.text: Buy the three-bedroom house on Ridge Road next year
Put all overtime pay onto the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking AI lands and forty when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so don't panic. Plenty of people at Tallow Hill will retire before it bites. For me it's a career change at forty, which people do all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm fine. Ten years of drilling money, a house mostly paid off, maybe kids by then. I'd still want a skill that robots need, but I don't have to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and go for leading hand in a couple of years, because that pays more and teaches me planning. I'd do the control room course when it opens. Then around year five or six I'd pick a second trade, probably electrical, and do it part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others. It feels like a normal career problem rather than a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change in your plans outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kids, probably. Lena and I have talked about starting a family around thirty. With ten years warning we'd still do that, we'd just make sure we're not stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk for you in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that I keep putting it off. Ten years can feel like forever until it's three. I'd write it down, a date for the course, so I actually do it.

say: There's **time**, so there's no reason to panic.
A **career change at forty** is something people do all the time.
think: Ten years of **drilling pay** leaves him with a house mostly paid off.
He still wants a **skill robots need**, but there's no rush.
do: Go for **leading hand** within two years for more pay and planning experience.
Pick up a **part-time trade**, probably electrical, around year five or six.
feel: **Calm**, more like a normal career question than a crisis.
S4.quote: Ten years can feel like forever until it's three.
fieldNote: He calls himself fine, but his own risk is **putting it off**, which keeps him uneasy.
Family plans around **thirty** stay in place with ten years of warning.
He would set a **written date** for retraining to guard against delay.

steps.text: Apply for leading hand on the drill crew within two years
Write down a start date for a part-time electrical course
Start a family with Lena around age thirty as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Not because of money, we'd be okay for a while, but because there's no time to retrain before the robots show up. What would help is if the mine paid for the retraining, like they do when a pit closes, and if the trade courses had places for people like me instead of a two-year waiting list.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the people who aren't young. I'm twenty-seven with no kids, I can bounce. Some of the guys on my crew are fifty with a mortgage and two kids in school. They have no plan B at all. They're the ones I'd want you to talk to.

headlineQuote: I'm twenty-seven with no kids, I can bounce. Some of the guys on my crew are fifty with a mortgage and two kids in school.
portrait: Wei, 27, runs a **blasthole drill** at Tallow Hill, a large open-pit copper mine.
He lives with **Lena (his partner)**, a nurse, and they are saving to buy a house.
Steady and practical, he plans to train for the **control room** before he is asked to.
With **two years** of warning he'd retrain in electrical work and pause the house purchase.
With **ten years** he relaxes, but admits his real risk is putting it off.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to retrain before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: The mine **paying for retraining**, as it does when a pit closes.
**Trade courses** with open places instead of two-year waiting lists.
